question: Freedom of religion and the principle of non-discrimination are fundamental values of the European Union, enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. The Copts face significant challenges regarding access to suitable facilities for practising their religion, with limited availability of churches exclusively for their community.

The priests of the Coptic Church, who can marry and have families, do not benefit from state subsidies, unlike other religious groups, which puts such families in economically precarious situations. In the light of the above: 1.
What actions can the Commission take to support Member States in ensuring that the Coptic community has fair access to suitable places of worship, thus respecting the principle of religious freedom?

What initiatives at EU level can encourage Member States to treat all religious communities equally and in a non-discriminatory manner, including providing adequate state subsidies for priests of all faiths, in line with the principles of equality and non-discrimination?

How can the Commission work with national authorities to acknowledge and respond to the economic and organisational challenges facing the Coptic community in Europe, thus promoting integration and respect for the rights of religious minorities?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2024) The Commission is committed to the protection of freedom of thought, conscience and religion as well as the principle of non-discrimination, as enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the Charter).

The Commission is also committed to pursue its regular dialogue with religious and non-confessional organisations based on Article 17 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). The Special Envoy on freedom of religion or belief also engages in dialogues with countries outside the EU on these matters.
According to Article 17 TFEU, the Union respects and does not prejudice the status under national law of churches and religious associations or communities in the Member States.

Moreover, the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing European Union law (Article 51(1) of the Charter) and Article 6(1) of the Treaty on European Union states that, ‘[t]he provisions of the Charter shall not extend in any way the competences of the Union as defined in the Treaties.
’ On the basis of the information provided, it does not appear that the matter to which the Honourable Member refers is related to the implementation of EU law.

In the present case, it is thus for national authorities, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations, including under the European Convention on Human Rights.
